::: {.chapter-lead}
Between GPT-2 and contemporary LLM systems, progress cannot be reduced to increasing parameter counts or replacing one architecture with another. It combines several changes: scale and data, in-context learning, post-training, input and output modalities, additional inference-time compute, efficiency, and integration into systems that use tools. This page provides a cross-cutting framework; it is not a technical specification of proprietary models.
:::

## Read evolution along several axes

A generation-by-generation comparison is useful for orientation, but it hides the fact that several dimensions evolve in parallel. At least six axes should be distinguished:

1. **Scale and data** — parameters, training tokens, data quality and diversity, and compute budget.
2. **Learning procedure** — pretraining, instruction tuning, preference learning, and other forms of post-training.
3. **Architecture and efficiency** — attention, dense or expert-based architectures, cache management, memory costs, and latency.
4. **Modalities** — processing text, images, audio, or other inputs and outputs.
5. **Inference-time compute** — reasoning strategies, additional compute budgets, and verification.
6. **Surrounding system** — tools, orchestration, routing, asynchronous execution, and control during generation.

These axes are related but not interchangeable. An improvement observed in a product does not, by itself, establish a specific change to the neural network architecture.

## Milestones: GPT-2 to GPT-6

The table summarizes public information highlighted by the cited sources. It is not a controlled comparison: available information, evaluation protocols, and transparency differ across generations.

| Generation | Publicly documented highlights | Main takeaway |
|---|---|---|
| **GPT-2 (2019)** | Autoregressive Transformer pretrained to predict the next token; the largest model in the study had 1.5 billion parameters. | Demonstrated the potential of large-scale pretraining and zero-shot transfer, before the conversational post-training practices that later became common. |
| **GPT-3 (2020)** | 175 billion parameters; few-shot performance obtained by placing examples in the prompt, without updating weights for each evaluated task. | Made in-context learning a central property to study, distinct from fine-tuning. |
| **GPT-4 (2023)** | Multimodal model accepting text and image inputs and producing text; iterative alignment and evaluation work. | Modalities and alignment became visible dimensions of progress beyond text prediction alone. |
| **GPT-5 (2025)** | A unified system described as combining fast models and reasoning models, with a router selecting according to the request and its needs. | Reasoning and routing can be properties of system organization as well as of an individual network. |
| **GPT-6 (2026)** | API documentation describes, among other features, asynchronous tool calling and *mid-turn steering* through the Responses API over WebSocket. | Interaction between the model, application, and tools becomes an important part of observable behavior. |

**Reading caveat.** The ByteByteGo article is a useful pedagogical summary, but some of its statements compress complex topics. For example, GPT-2 already showed zero-shot transfer on some tasks; it would be inaccurate to say it could only continue text and had no question-answering capability. The GPT-3 paper explicitly documents few-shot use *without gradient updates*, whereas complete internal details of newer models are not all public.

## 1. From scale to in-context learning

Increasing model and corpus sizes contributed to improved measured performance on many tasks. But parameter count is only one dimension: token volume, data quality, training compute, architecture, and evaluation protocol also matter.

GPT-3 made **in-context learning** (ICL) particularly visible: examples placed in the prompt can guide model behavior without updating its parameters. It is therefore not fine-tuning performed for every request.

Further reading:
- [Scaling laws](scaling-laws.qmd) — empirical relationships between parameters, data, compute, and loss.
- [In-context learning](in-context-learning.qmd) — zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, and generalization limits.
- [Emergence](emergence.qmd) — the role of metrics, thresholds, and protocols in claims about emergent capabilities.

## 2. From pretraining to post-training

Pretraining learns statistical regularities from a corpus, often through autoregressive next-token prediction. By itself, it does not fully specify the conversational behavior expected from an assistant.

**Post-training** groups several families of procedures that adapt a pretrained model to particular uses and preferences:

- **Instruction tuning / SFT** (*supervised fine-tuning*): supervised adjustment on instruction-and-response examples.
- **RLHF** (*reinforcement learning from human feedback*): use of human preferences, often represented by a reward model, in an optimization procedure.
- **DPO** (*direct preference optimization*): direct optimization from preference data, without following exactly the classic pipeline involving a reward model and an RL loop.

These methods are neither synonyms nor necessarily used together. Their details, variants, and trade-offs deserve dedicated lessons. Avoid attributing a specific method to a model generation when public documentation does not confirm it.

Post-training does not replace the underlying predictive model: it changes the parameters or the way the model is trained in order to shape its outputs.

## 3. From text-only inputs to multimodal models

A multimodal model processes more than one data type, such as text and images. This does not necessarily mean that it uses one shared representation or a uniform architecture for every modality.

To understand a multimodal architecture, ask more specific questions:

- How is each modality encoded?
- At what level are representations combined?
- Does interaction use cross-attention, shared tokens, or another interface?
- Which modalities are accepted as inputs, and which can be produced as outputs?
- Which evaluations actually measure multimodal capabilities?

[Cross-attention](cross-attention.qmd) is an important mechanism to understand, but it is not a universal explanation of all multimodal architectures.

## 4. From learned computation to inference-time compute

Reasoning models highlight another dimension: spending more compute on solving a request, for example by generating intermediate steps, exploring several possibilities, or checking an answer.

This is often called **inference-time compute** or *test-time compute*. It refers to compute used during model operation, not a weight update as in training.

Distinguish:
- reasoning capabilities learned in the parameters during training;
- additional compute spent on a particular request;
- search, verification, or selection mechanisms;
- reasoning content exposed to a user, which is not necessarily a faithful trace of every internal computation.

Increasing the inference budget can improve some performance measures, but it costs latency and compute and does not guarantee a correct answer.

## 5. Architecture and efficiency: several independent levers

The evolution of LLM systems does not mean that the dense Transformer has simply been replaced by one new architecture. Several variants address different constraints:

- **Mixture of Experts (MoE)** activates a subset of experts for some tokens, with trade-offs involving capacity, routing, memory, and communication.
- **GQA / MQA** reduce the number of key/value groups relative to standard multi-head attention, notably to reduce KV-cache memory costs.
- **KV cache** avoids recomputing prefix keys and values at every decoding step.
- **Speculative decoding** uses an auxiliary model or mechanism to propose tokens, which are then checked by the target model through a procedure designed to preserve the intended distribution.

These techniques are not mutually exclusive and do not solve the same problem. Some target compute cost, others memory traffic, throughput, or latency.

Further reading: [Hybrid architectures](hybrid-llm-architectures.qmd) and [Computational complexity and parallelism](llm-computational-complexity.qmd).

## 6. From a model to a system that uses tools

A model that can produce a tool call does not necessarily execute the requested operation itself. In a typical integration, the application receives the call, executes the tool, and sends its result back to the model.

Agentic systems add an orchestration loop: interpret a goal, plan, call tools, inspect results, and possibly repeat. Distinguish:

- **tool calling**: a structured representation of a requested action;
- **tool execution**: the responsibility of the application or external service;
- **orchestration**: management of calls, results, errors, retries, and task state;
- **control**: the ability to modify or stop work and manage side effects.

GPT-6 documentation illustrates two system capabilities:
- asynchronous tool calling lets the model continue independent work while the application executes a tool;
- *mid-turn steering* lets additional instructions be sent during a response over WebSocket. It does not rewrite output already emitted or cancel tools that have already started.

These features do not mean the application delegates responsibility for execution to the model. Tools, permissions, results, and side effects remain the application's responsibility.

## What this evolution does not establish

The GPT-2 to GPT-6 milestones are not a controlled experiment. The models are not compared with identical data, compute, objectives, and protocols. Public information is also uneven: reports and system cards document some properties, but do not necessarily reveal parameter counts, data, detailed architectures, or training recipes.

Avoid inferring a specific architectural mechanism from a generation name or a product capability. For every claim, ask:

1. Is this a published model property, an API feature, or the author's interpretation?
2. Which primary source documents it?
3. Which metric and protocol support the capability claim?
4. Can the model's contribution be separated from routing, tools, prompts, and the application?
5. Which details remain unknown?

## Synthesis

LLM evolution is best read as the convergence of several axes, not as a simple succession of sizes or architectures:

- pretraining and scale build base capabilities;
- post-training shapes behavior;
- context enables temporary adaptation without parameter updates;
- multimodality broadens the kinds of information processed;
- inference-time compute allocates additional resources to selected requests;
- tools and orchestration turn the model into a component of a larger system.

The most useful mental model is therefore **a predictive model at the core of a system**, whose observable capabilities also depend on its training, inference budget, interfaces, and execution environment.

## References and resources

### Pedagogical overview
- ByteByteGo, [GPT-2 to GPT-6: What Actually Changed](https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/222752055/gpt-2-to-gpt-6-what-actually-changed) — starting point for this synthesis; specific claims are qualified and cross-checked below.

### Primary sources and documentation
- Radford et al. (2019), [Better Language Models and Their Implications](https://openai.com/index/better-language-models/) — GPT-2 overview.
- Brown et al. (2020), [Language Models are Few-Shot Learners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165) — GPT-3 and in-context learning.
- Ouyang et al. (2022), [Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155) — supervised instruction tuning and RLHF.
- Rafailov et al. (2023), [Direct Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290) — preference optimization without a separately trained reward model in the basic formulation.
- Fedus et al. (2021), [Switch Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) — sparse mixture-of-experts routing.
- Ainslie et al. (2023), [GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245) — grouped-query attention.
- Leviathan et al. (2023), [Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192) — speculative decoding.
- OpenAI (2023), [GPT-4](https://openai.com/index/gpt-4-research/) — multimodal capabilities and alignment.
- OpenAI (2025), [GPT-5 System Card](https://openai.com/index/gpt-5-system-card/) — fast models, reasoning, and routing.
- OpenAI, [Using GPT-6](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model?model=gpt-6-astra) — documented GPT-6 API capabilities.
- OpenAI, [Async tool calling](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/async-tool-calling) — asynchronous execution contract.
- OpenAI, [Mid-turn steering](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/steering) — steering an ongoing response.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does GPT-3 illustrate in-context learning rather than fine-tuning for every few-shot task?
2. Why should post-training not be confused with pretraining?
3. An API exposes asynchronous tool calling: what remains the application's responsibility?
4. Is a benchmark improvement enough to demonstrate an architectural change? Why?
5. Classify MoE, KV cache, RLHF, and inference-time compute by their primary axis.
